title: The Hidden Cost of Keeping the Old
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: A third-grade teacher documents, hour by hour, the real cost of her district adopting a science-of-reading-aligned Acadience benchmark without retiring the older assessment system it was meant to replace. She shows that she alone assessed eight students on eight measures — including ORF, Retell, the CORE Phonics Survey, and Acadience Math — in 2.5 total hours, producing instructionally actionable data she could use the very next school day. By contrast, her school's separate intervention (AIS) team spent 30 staff-hours across five teachers and two days administering guided reading levels and Fry sight-word checklists to her class alone, tools she argues were never designed to diagnose why a student struggles and that delay the start of intervention instruction until nearly October. Her central argument is that keeping both systems running in parallel is not a neutral, cautious transition but an active choice with a real cost paid disproportionately by students who most need instructional time, including the six pupils with IEPs in her own class. She frames this as a case study in why 'deimplementation' — deciding what to stop doing — must be built into reform plans from the outset rather than deferred indefinitely to avoid discomfort among staff. The piece closes by insisting that a genuinely data-driven school system must let assessment data justify retiring redundant practices, not just justify adopting new ones.

quotes: Total time: 2.5 hours. Total assessments: 35. Total teachers required: 1. And every one of those 35 data points is instructionally actionable.
That's 30 staff-hours to complete 28 assessments. Thirty hours.
Guided reading levels and sight-word checklists don't tell me why a student is struggling. They don't tell me what phonics skill needs to be taught.
Time is the one resource within a school day that we cannot manufacture more of. Every hour spent on redundant testing is an hour that cannot be spent on instruction.
We need fidelity to the evidence, not fidelity to a program.
If we're serious about protecting instructional time, deimplementation has to be part of the plan from day one—not something we get around to "eventually.
We have to change the adults' behaviors to support the student's outcomes.
